timeline.title: Born in Erode
timeline.text: Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 in the house of his mother's father in Erode. His family was poor. His father was a clerk to a cloth merchant in the temple town of Kumbakonam, where Ramanujan grew up.

timeline.title: A childhood illness
timeline.text: In December 1889 the small boy caught smallpox and recovered. Afterwards he moved for a time with his mother to Kanchipuram, near Madras.

timeline.title: First school
timeline.text: In 1892, aged about five, he started at a simple local school. Sources differ on the details and the later schools he moved between before the Town High School.

timeline.title: Top of the district
timeline.text: In 1897 he came first in the Tanjore District in the primary examination. He joined the Town High School in Kumbakonam, where he met formal mathematics for the first time.

timeline.title: The book that woke him
timeline.text: A friend borrowed for him G. S. Carr's Synopsis, a dense list of formulas, from the college library. He set out to prove every result himself. His early biographers wrote: "It was this book that awakened his genius."

timeline.title: A scholarship lost
timeline.text: He won a scholarship to the Government College in Kumbakonam. But he spent his lessons on mathematics, failed the other subjects, and lost the scholarship. Hardy later blamed mainly his weak English.

timeline.title: Running away
timeline.text: Upset at his failure, he left home and travelled north into the Telugu country. He stayed about a month in Rajahmundry before coming back to Kumbakonam.

timeline.title: No degree
timeline.text: He enrolled at Pachaiyappa's College in Madras, passed in mathematics, but failed the First Arts examination in December 1906. Wikipedia says he failed again a year later. He never earned a regular degree and kept working alone, filling his notebooks.

timeline.title: Marriage
timeline.text: On 14 July 1909 he married Janaki (Janakiammal), who was about ten. Now he needed a steady job.

timeline.title: Looking for work, notebook in hand
timeline.text: He visited V. Ramaswami Aiyar, founder of the Indian Mathematical Society, to ask for a clerk's job. Aiyar saw the notebook and felt such talent would be wasted in an office. He sent Ramanujan on to friends in Madras.

timeline.title: A patron is convinced
timeline.text: The official R. Ramachandra Rao met him in December 1910. He later remembered a poor young man with a frayed notebook and shining eyes, who wanted only enough to live on so he could do research. Rao paid his costs for a time.

timeline.title: First paper
timeline.text: His first long article, "Some Properties of Bernoulli's Numbers", appeared in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society in 1911.

timeline.title: Clerk at the Port Trust
timeline.text: He became an accounts clerk at the Madras Port Trust for 30 rupees a month. Sources disagree on the start date: Wikipedia and MacTutor say 1 March 1912; his 1927 memoir says 9 February 1912. His managers liked mathematics and encouraged him.

timeline.title: The letter to Hardy
timeline.text: After two other Cambridge mathematicians returned his papers without comment, he wrote to G. H. Hardy at Trinity College. The letter came with pages of theorems. Hardy first wondered if it was a prank, then decided it was genuine and remarkable.

timeline.title: Hardy replies
timeline.text: Hardy answered on 8 February 1913 with interest. He asked to see proofs of some of the claims, and he began trying to bring Ramanujan to Cambridge.

timeline.title: Paid to do mathematics
timeline.text: In May 1913 the University of Madras gave him a two-year research scholarship, 75 rupees a month. For the first time he could do mathematics as his job.

timeline.title: Sailing for England
timeline.text: At first he refused to travel, partly for religious reasons. His mother agreed after a dream, and the university gave him a scholarship of 250 pounds a year. He sailed on 17 March 1914.

timeline.title: Arrival at Trinity
timeline.text: He reached London on 14 April with E. H. Neville and soon moved into rooms at Trinity College. Hardy found him brilliant but missing much of modern mathematics, and set about teaching him proof.

timeline.title: Formulas for pi
timeline.text: His paper "Modular equations and approximations to pi", mostly Indian work, came out in 1914. It held striking new series for pi. Similar series are behind some of the fastest methods for computing pi today.

timeline.title: Highly composite numbers
timeline.text: He published a long paper on numbers that have more divisors than any smaller number. Hardy called the analysis "most remarkable". Keeping to his strict religious diet in wartime England was hard.

timeline.title: A Cambridge degree
timeline.text: Cambridge gave him a Bachelor of Arts by Research for his work on highly composite numbers. The degree was later renamed the PhD.

timeline.title: The tau function
timeline.text: In "On certain arithmetical functions" he made three guesses about a number sequence now called the tau function. Mordell proved two in 1917. The hardest was proved by Pierre Deligne in 1974.

timeline.title: Serious illness
timeline.text: In 1917 he fell seriously ill and spent much of the next two years in nursing homes. Because of the war, sailing home was too risky. He kept working whenever he could.

timeline.title: Counting partitions
timeline.text: With Hardy he published a formula that estimates how many ways a number can be split into a sum of smaller numbers. It was accurate enough to give exact answers. Hardy and MacMahon both counted it among his best work.

timeline.title: Fellow of the Royal Society
timeline.text: He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. His 1927 memoir dates it 28 February and calls him the first Indian Fellow. Wikipedia and MacTutor say the election was confirmed on 2 May 1918, and Wikipedia says he was the second Indian, after Ardaseer Cursetjee in 1841.

timeline.title: Fellow of Trinity
timeline.text: He became the first Indian elected a Fellow of Trinity College, with six years of paid research and no duties. MacTutor gives the date as 10 October instead of 13 October.

timeline.title: Home to India
timeline.text: Hoping the climate would help him recover, he left England on 27 February 1919. The 1927 memoir says he landed at Bombay on 27 March; MacTutor says he arrived on 13 March. The University of Madras gave him an allowance for five more years.

timeline.title: The last letter
timeline.text: Though very ill, he wrote to Hardy about new functions he called mock theta functions. The 1927 memoir says this work was done in his last months. It took mathematicians about 80 years to fully understand them.

timeline.place: Chetput, Madras, (Chennai, India) or Kumbakonam, (Tamil Nadu, India)
timeline.title: Death at 32
timeline.text: Ramanujan died on 26 April 1920. Sources disagree on the place: his Indian memoir says Chetput in Madras, while Hardy and MacTutor say Kumbakonam. The illness was long thought to be tuberculosis; a 1994 study suggested a liver infection instead.

timeline.title: The Collected Papers
timeline.text: Hardy and others published his Collected Papers, with his letters and two memoirs of his life. The editors wrote that his notebooks held much that "should certainly be published".

timeline.title: The lost notebook found
timeline.text: In spring 1976 George Andrews found a bundle of over 100 pages of Ramanujan's last-year work in the Wren Library at Trinity College. It had been out of sight for decades. It was published in 1987-88.

timeline.title: National Mathematics Day
timeline.text: At the University of Madras, India's prime minister declared his birthday, 22 December, National Mathematics Day, marking his 125th birth anniversary.

feature.title: Famous results, simply explained
feature.lead: Ramanujan wrote down nearly 3,900 results, most without proofs. Here are some of the best known, in plain words.

items.label: 1729, the taxicab number
items.text: Hardy visited him in hospital and said his taxi number, 1729, seemed dull. Ramanujan said no: it is the smallest number you can write as the sum of two cubes in two different ways (1 cubed + 12 cubed, and 9 cubed + 10 cubed). The fact was known since 1657, and was also in his notebook years before.

items.label: Counting partitions
items.text: A partition is a way to split a number into a sum. The number 4 has five: 4, 3+1, 2+2, 2+1+1 and 1+1+1+1. The count grows enormous very fast. With Hardy he found a formula that predicts it so well it gives exact answers.

items.label: Patterns of 5, 7 and 11
items.text: By working out many examples, he noticed that the number of partitions of 4, 9, 14, 19 and so on (every fifth number) is always divisible by 5. Similar rules hold for 7 and 11. Hardy said he found these patterns from numerical examples.

items.label: Rogers-Ramanujan identities
items.text: Two formulas he found on his own before 1913. One says: the ways to split a number into parts that differ by at least 2 equal the ways to split it into parts ending in a 1, 4, 6 or 9 (one more or less than a multiple of 5). L. J. Rogers had proved them in 1894; the two published a joint proof in 1919.

items.label: Fast formulas for pi
items.text: His 1914 paper gave new series for pi that close in on the right value very quickly. Hardy praised them. Related series are used by modern computers to work out pi to trillions of digits.

items.label: Highly composite numbers
items.text: Numbers like 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 have more divisors than any smaller number. He studied them in a long paper that earned his Cambridge degree. Hardy said it showed his "extraordinary mastery" of inequalities.

items.label: The tau function
items.text: He looked at a special sequence of numbers (1, -24, 252, and on) and guessed three rules about it. Mordell proved two the next year. The last, a size limit, was proved by Pierre Deligne in 1974 as part of work that won a Fields Medal.

items.label: Bernoulli numbers
items.text: His first long paper, published in India, found new properties of a famous sequence of fractions used across mathematics.

items.label: Mock theta functions
items.text: In his last letter to Hardy he described 17 new functions that behave almost, but not quite, like older ones. Only in 2002 did Sander Zwegers explain what they really are. They are now used even in the physics of black holes.

items.label: The notebooks
items.text: From his teens he wrote his results in notebooks, mostly without proofs. Bruce Berndt spent years checking them and argues he could prove most of them. They were printed in facsimile in 1957.

items.label: The lost notebook
items.text: Over 600 formulas from his final year, on loose sheets. They were found in the Wren Library at Trinity College in 1976 and filled five volumes of proofs by George Andrews and Bruce Berndt (2005 to 2018).

works.title: The notebooks
works.text: The notebooks of results he kept from his teens, mostly without proofs. Printed in facsimile in 1957.

works.title: Some Properties of Bernoulli's Numbers
works.text: His first long paper, in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society.

works.title: Letters to Hardy
works.text: His letters of 1913 from Madras, packed with theorems, which brought him to Cambridge. Parts are printed in the Collected Papers.

works.title: Modular equations and approximations to pi
works.text: Series and approximations for pi, mostly worked out in India; the basis of modern fast pi formulas.

works.title: Highly composite numbers
works.text: A long study of numbers with record numbers of divisors; the basis of his Cambridge degree.

works.title: On certain arithmetical functions
works.text: Introduced his three conjectures about the tau function, fully proved only in 1974.

works.title: Asymptotic formulae in combinatory analysis (with Hardy)
works.text: The Hardy-Ramanujan formula for counting partitions, made exact by Rademacher in 1937.

works.title: Rogers-Ramanujan identities (with L. J. Rogers)
works.text: A joint proof of two partition formulas that Ramanujan had found on his own.

works.title: Congruence properties of partitions
works.text: His patterns for partitions with 5, 7 and 11. A further paper on them appeared after his death in 1921.

works.title: Last letter on mock theta functions
works.text: His letter of 12 January 1920 listing 17 mock theta functions.

works.title: The lost notebook
works.text: Over 600 formulas from his last year, rediscovered in 1976 and published in 1987-88.

works.title: Collected Papers of Srinivasa Ramanujan
works.text: All his published papers, with letters and memoirs, edited by Hardy, Seshu Aiyar and Wilson.
